Currently, new users are granted 10 votes to allocate per day. Once they reach a comment score of 20, they are then granted an infinite number of votes to allocate per day. We can express this rule as follows:

votes_per_day = comment_score < 20 then 10 else Infinity

I see allowing a single user to cast an infinite number of votes per day to be highly problematic. With no upper limit or scarcity imposed on the supply and act of voting, I believe that users will view a single vote as holding little to no value.

When a single vote holds little value, I believe users will cast them carelessly. This could encourage users to engage in activities such as the blanket upvoting of every comment in a thread which remotely aligns with their subjective value and political views, while ignoring the thought and effort put into the contents of a comment prior to upvoting it.

When individual voters exercise low standards during the act of granting a vote, I believe that the aggregate value generated by the information ranking and filtering algorithms dependent upon these votes will suffer.

One suggestion on how to fix this would be to always impose a finite cap on the number of votes a single user can cast per day, no matter how large and improbable it is that a single user will actually reach it. One possible way to do this would be to change the above rule to the following:

votes_per_day = max(10, comment_score / 2)

What this implies is that the greater one's comment score, the greater the number of votes one can cast per day, while still allowing users with less than 20 comment score to have a guaranteed minimum of 10 votes.

Suppose we were to plug in some numbers:

comment-score votes-per-day
0 10
20 10
40 20
80 40
160 80
320 160

What we see is that new users would be gradually granted additional power the more they contributed. This would disincentivize new users from viewing the initial 20 comment score hump as simply an artificial barrier to be broken and gamed as quickly as possible. It would incentivize new users wishing to gain influence to instead take the time to submit high quality comments and posts.

Refactoring the code to allow such an algorithm would also give the administrators an additional control for tweaking site experience, in a manner which would competitively differentiate it from Reddit.
Deterministically Scaling Voting Quota Applied Equally to All Accounts

I think that it might be worth exploring the use of ratios in the modifier formula.

For example, a persons:

Link/Point ratio

Comment/Point ratio

This might be a valuable metric for determining the value of an individuals contribution to the community at large. Of course there is the issue of individuals accruing lots of downvotes for saying something unpopular but the law of averages should balance this shit out over the long term as long as there are at least X number of links/comments to begin with.

I think this is definitely be worth exploring, but I am unsure on how to best combine the two terms and what a proper ratio should be. Suppose we were to add a link_score term via addition:

votes_per_day = max(10, link_score / 8 + comment_score / 2)

My primary concern with such a rule would be that someone could submit only news articles, up their link_score, and then sell the account to a black hat marketer. Since they would not have had to submit many comments and examples of their style of writing to achieve this high score, users may not notice if the account was compromised and sold to someone else for marketing purposes.

However, if a different ratio than 1/8 was used for link_score, or different operation for combining the two terms was used, then this problem could perhaps be ammeliorated to some extent. It's also possible that if were to plug in some actual numbers, we would find my concern unfounded.

One idea for evaluating and selecting new formulas, would be to create a public spreadsheet of mock user data, including both comment-score and link-score columns, and then create a votes-per-day column for each new votes-per-day formula that is suggested.

This could then perhaps be used to develop a series of publicly viewable graphs, which are then debated or put to a vote in a future /v/ideasforvoat post. The admins may have a better idea on how to organize this than me, however.

This post is a bit of a rough draft, as I had some unfortunate trouble organizing the concepts. The information is there, however; and this post is meant to prompt discussion more than anything else, so I encourage any and all feedback.

The anthropological definition of a patriarchal society is a society in which men, as a group, hold more power, wealth, and prestige than women do. These societies are typically Patrilocal, meaning that families are organized into living spaces around a single household patriarch. (This is opposed to Matrilocal societies, where families are organized around a single household matriarch.) It should be noted that the recent trend in western society is towards "neolocal" organization, meaning that once coming of age, people establish their own households. This is a relatively new and rare behavior.

One must ask why this tendency exists. The popular feminist explanation is that men designed society in a way that would unfairly serve their interests, but this is a superficial observation that does not hold up under scrutiny. To accept this explanation, one must believe that for the vast majority of history 50% of the population was universally successful in oppressing and exploiting the other 50% of the population with no sort of cohesive revolution or disobedience, political or otherwise, until the last half of the 19th century. (And that's speaking generously.)

What seems more likely is that for some reason, this particular gendered organization of power was mutually beneficial to both genders.

Due to a variety of factors, competitive societies have defined the masculine gender role as a competitive space, creating a "male hierarchy", with a small elite class of extremely wealthy and powerful men, and a much larger male population with little to no power or wealth. Simultaneously, these societies have defined the feminine gender role as a cooperative and passive space, creating a cohesive female population with little competition or hierarchy. This is not a model that is necessarily present in all or even most cultures and societies across the world and throughout history, but it is a model that can be observed in all of the largest and most powerful civilizations in history: Ancient Rome, Imperial China, Imperialist England, and of course the United States of America. Why is this a model that is so common among the "Apex Predators" of history? Because this model is the one that is and has been the most "mechanically effective" for preserving and propagating a society. If we look at a society like an organism, the "mutation" of this gender model is one most conducive to the survival and success of that society: a natural adaption.

This so-called oppression of women makes sense: Female-bodied people are indisputably more valuable for reproduction, and allowing them into spheres where they would participate in often very violent and dangerous political competition could get them hurt or killed. The death of a man is simply not the logistical setback to a society that the death of a woman is. Men have very little inherent value when it comes to reproduction, and so there is much less at stake when they risk their lives and health competing.

The findings of a recent study suggest that approximately 8,000 years ago, "shortly" after the invention of agriculture and the dawn of complex civilizations, only one man had offspring for every seventeen women. From the article:

"...hypothesizes that somehow, only a few men accumulated lots of wealth and power, leaving nothing for others. These men could then pass their wealth on to their sons, perpetuating this pattern of elitist reproductive success."

This observation lends support to the concept of a large competitive male hierarchy, with men at the top enjoying the most wealth, power, and reproductive capability. Notice in the graph below that this is a trend which began immediately and drastically as civilizations began building permanent settlements and relying on agriculture as their primary subsistence method. Why would stationary civilizations lead to a spike in male competition? Could it be the introduction of complex and long-term warfare? Political leadership in the very early days would have likely been a very violent occupation. There were perks to power, but there were very real and present risks as well.

This realization begs the question: to what extent is the male hierarchy still alive and active? Additionally, Can we look at the men who make up the vast majority of the homeless, the incarcerated, and the victims of homicide as the "low end" of the male hierarchy, just as we can look at male politicians and CEO's as the "high end"? Furthermore, Has feminism helped us expose and dismantle the male hierarchy in any reasonable way? Isn't addressing the male hierarchy the logical next step in achieving gender justice for both men AND women?
The "Male Hierarchy" in the Context of Reproduction

The concept of the alpha male is a well-known thing. It is seen in humans and animals as well. It is natural for all females, regardless of their genetics, to seek out the best possible mate because they are the ones that get to choose what genes ultimately are passed on.

Edit- I do not necessarily think that the hierarchy is something that must be dismantled. Alphas are the ones that create the best humans in future generations. I think that there are different types of alphas, however. There are the intelligent ones, the athletic ones, and the assholes that get both.

This post was meant primarily as an alternative to the feminist description of certain societies as "patriarchal": I meant to demonstrate that the defining of a society as patriarchal typically ignores the presence of extreme male competition. To define a society as a patriarchy is to see both the male and female population as two consolidated and stationary classes, one above the other. I meant to suggest that instead, women typically make up a consolidated and stationary class while men fall into an extremely competitive and fluidly changing class; free to rise to the top or fall to the bottom.

I do not necessarily think that the hierarchy is something that must be dismantled.

While I believe it is natural for certain people to be considered more desirable mates than others, (and indeed, this is not a facet of human organization that we can dismantle or transcend without a radical evolution of human nature) it seems to me as though the definition of what you term an "alpha" has been broadening as society grows more complex.

I believe that the next phase of the gender discussion is the systematic identification and revocation of what I term our cultural "gender ethos"; expectations and demands which we place upon people based solely on their gender. This is something that I feel feminists have failed to do, owing largely to their lack of respect for and attention to a male perspective. While I do not believe "attraction equity" can or should ever be attained, an auxiliary effect of "dismantling" the gender ethos would be an increased liberty for men to act effeminate or non-masculine without losing the respect of his friends and romantic prospects.
